To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the time delays for gravitational waves in dark matter emulators are reduced relative to the delays for photons or neutrinos, that the time delay for GRB 200701 is reduced by 0.3 to 0.6 seconds, that the delay for SN 1989a is reduced by 3 to 6 seconds, and that the delay for Sco X1 is reduced by 2 to 3 seconds.

the time delay between gravitational waves and photons for GRB 07-201 is expected to be 0.3 +/- 0.1 ms; the delay for Sco-X1 is expected to be less than 0.2 ms and the delay for SN 1988a is expected to be between 0.1 and 0.3 ms.

the Shapiro delays of photons and neutrinos are larger than those of gravitational waves in dark matter emulators by a factor which is of order the square root of the dark matter to baryonic matter ratio.

a class of modified gravities which have been proposed to account for the absence of dark matter in galaxies and galaxy clusters, and which are known as ‘dark matter emulators’.

the time lag is likely to be less than 1 s, and that the probability of it being less than 0.1 s is greater than 0.99.
the dark matter emulator is not excluded by the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dark matter emulators predict that the time lags for gravitational waves from the same sources as photons and neutrinos should be smaller than those predicted by general relativity.

dark matter emulators are a promising class of models for explaining dark matter, and that the gravitational waves from a dark matter emulator will be distinguishable from the gravitational waves of standard general relativity by their reduced Shapiro delays, with a detectable effect for GRB 170201.
the expected time lag between gravitational waves and photons from the same source is 1.4-2.4 ms, with a 95% confidence interval.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the difference in Shapiro delays between gravitational waves and ordinary particles is likely to be measurable for Sco-X1 with a time resolution of about 0.1 seconds, and for SN 1986a with a time resolution better than 1 second.
the difference in Shapiro delays between photons and gravitational waves is a powerful probe of dark matter, with a sensitivity which is comparable to that of other methods.

the time delay between photons and gravitational waves can be used to constrain dark matter emulators in the same way as the time delay between gravitational waves and neutrinos can be used to probe the nature of dark matter.
